translationRepairs: The Marquis of Weiqi, Dou Ying, was a nephew of Empress Dowager Dou, consort of Emperor Wen.
The Marquis of Weiqi, Dou Ying, was the son of a male cousin of Empress Dou, consort of Emperor Wen.
孝文后 names Wen's empress rather than a dowager, and 從兄子 is specifically the son of an elder male cousin.

When Emperor Jing died, the Crown Prince was enthroned that very day and assumed authority. Many of the measures taken to pacify and secure the realm were devised by Tian Fen and his retainers. Tian Fen's younger brother Tian Sheng—both being brothers of the Empress Dowager—were enfeoffed in the third year after Emperor Jing's death: Tian Fen as the Marquis of Wu'an, and Tian Sheng as the Marquis of Zhouyang.

When Emperor Jing died, the Crown Prince was enthroned that very day and assumed authority. Many of the measures taken to pacify and secure the realm were devised by Tian Fen and his retainers. Tian Fen's younger brother Tian Sheng—both being brothers of the Empress Dowager—were enfeoffed in the third year of Emperor Jing's later reign: Tian Fen as the Marquis of Wu'an, and Tian Sheng as the Marquis of Zhouyang.
孝景後三年 is Jing's later-reign third year (141 BC), coinciding with his death, not a date three years after that death.

When Emperor Jing died, the Crown Prince was enthroned that same day and assumed authority. Much of the pacification and stabilization was planned by Tian Fen and his retainers. Fen's younger brother Tian Sheng—both being brothers of the Empress Dowager—were in the third year after Emperor Jing enfeoffed: Fen as the Marquis of Wu'an, Sheng as the Marquis of Zhouyang.

When Emperor Jing died, the Crown Prince was enthroned that same day and assumed authority. Much of the pacification and stabilization was planned by Tian Fen and his retainers. Fen's younger brother Tian Sheng—both being brothers of the Empress Dowager—were in Jing's later third year enfeoffed: Fen as the Marquis of Wu'an, Sheng as the Marquis of Zhouyang.
孝景後三年 is Jing's later third year, not 'the third year after Emperor Jing'.
I also want to appoint officials.
The literal field is untranslated romanization rather than an English rendering of 吾亦欲除吏.
Guan Fu, styled General Guan, was a native of Yingyin.
General Guan Fu was a native of Yingyin.
灌將軍夫 juxtaposes the title 灌將軍 with the name 夫; it is not a courtesy-name (styled) construction.
The people of Yingchuan then sang of it, saying, "When the Ying runs clear, the Guan clan is at peace;
The children of Yingchuan then sang of it, saying, "When the Ying runs clear, the Guan clan is at peace;
Chinese 潁川兒 means children of Yingchuan; idiomatic 'people' widens the singers.
The Marquis of Weiqi was greatly disappointed and said, "Though I am an old servant cast aside, and though you, General, are noble, can you seize by power!"
The Marquis of Weiqi was greatly disappointed and said, "Though I am an old servant cast aside, and though you, General, are noble, can you really seize it by force of your position?"
English drops the object of 奪 and the rhetorical force of 寧可.
Guan Fu was angry and, with a mocking laugh, said, "You are a noble man, General—leave it to you!"
Guan Fu was angry and, with a mocking laugh, said, "You are a noble man, General—drain it!"
屬之 at a toast urges drinking the cup, not leaving the matter to the addressee.
During Emperor Jing's reign, the Marquis of Weiqi had often received a testamentary edict saying, "When matters are inconvenient, report to the throne at your discretion."
During Emperor Jing's reign, the Marquis of Weiqi had previously received a testamentary edict saying, "When matters are inconvenient, report to the throne at your discretion."
常受遺詔 is the established previously/once reading for one testamentary edict, not repeated receipt.
